
--- PAGE 1 ---
The eﬀect of insuﬃcient quadriceps strength on gait
after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
Michael Lewek a
, Katherine Rudolph a
, Michael Axe a,b
, Lynn Snyder-Mackler a,*
a
Department of Physical Therapy, 301 McKinly Lab, University of Delaware, Newark, DE 19716, USA
b
First State Orthopedics, 4745 Ogletown-Stanton Road, Suite 225, Newark, DE, USA
Received 16 October 2000; accepted 8 October 2001
Abstract
Objective. To determine the eﬀect of quadriceps strength and joint stability on gait patterns after anterior cruciate ligament injury
and reconstruction.
Design. Cross-sectional comparative study in which four groups underwent motion analysis with surface electromyography.
Background. Individuals following anterior cruciate ligament rupture often demonstrate reduced knee angles and moments
during the early stance phase of gait. Alterations in gait can neither be ascribed to instability nor to quadriceps weakness alone when
both are present.
Methods. Twenty-eight individuals with complete anterior cruciate ligament rupture (10 patients with acute rupture, 8 patients
following reconstruction with quadriceps strength >90% of the uninvolved side [strong-anterior cruciate ligament reconstructed
group], and 10 patients after reconstruction with quadriceps strength <80% of the uninvolved side [weak-anterior cruciate ligament
reconstructed group]), and 10 uninjured subjects underwent an examination of their lower extremity to collect kinematics, kinetics,
and electromyography during walking and jogging. Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction was arthroscopically assisted and a
double loop semitendinosis-gracilis autograft or allograft was used as a graft source. All reconstructed subjects had stable knees, full
range of motion, and no eﬀusion or pain at the time of testing (more than three months after surgery).
Results. Knee angles and moments of the strong group were indistinguishable from the uninjured group during early stance of
both walking and jogging. The weak subjects had reduced knee angles and moments during walking, and jogged similarly to the
deﬁcient subjects. Regression analysis revealed a signiﬁcant eﬀect between early stance phase knee angles and moments and
quadriceps strength during both walking and jogging.
Conclusion. Inadequate quadriceps strength contributes to altered gait patterns following anterior cruciate ligament recon-
struction.
Relevance
Rapid strengthening following anterior cruciate ligament injury or reconstruction may contribute to a safe return to high-level
activities. Ó 2002 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
Keywords: Quadriceps; Anterior cruciate ligament; Gait; Knee; Quadriceps avoidance
1. Introduction
Injury to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is
common amongst both regular participants in sports and
other active individuals, and precipitates excessive an-
terior tibio-femoral laxity [1]. An inability to control this
laxity results in joint instability and is usually manifested
as an episode of giving way, a common complaint
among individuals who are ACL deﬁcient [2–4]. Re-
search has shown that the amount of joint laxity is
not associated with a patient’s instability following an
ACL rupture, so the terms laxity and instability are
not synonymous [5,6]. Many patients require recon-
struction of the ACL to reduce the symptoms of in-
stability and allow a return to high levels of activity [1].
Individuals who experience instability with ACL
rupture do so when the injured limb accepts the weight
of the body in early stance. During weight acceptance,
the limb accepts full support of the body and attenuates
shock through knee ﬂexion that is controlled by an
www.elsevier.com/locate/clinbiomech

--- PAGE 2 ---
eccentric contraction of the quadriceps. When people
experience knee instability, they alter their movement
patterns at this point in the gait cycle through reduced
knee ﬂexion and reduced internal knee extensor mo-
ments [7,8]. These gait alterations may result from the
unwillingness to fully activate the quadriceps muscles at
a range close to full knee extension. Berchuck and An-
driacchi [7] termed the reduced knee extensor moment
‘‘quadriceps avoidance’’ because near full extension, a
quadriceps contraction may lead to anterior tibial
translation [9,10] that could initiate an episode of giving
way. The reduced knee moment, however, could repre-
sent either a reduction in quadriceps activation, or an
increase in ﬂexor activity provided by the hamstrings [2],
or the gastrocnemius [11] and EMG data must be used
to fully understand the implications of a reduced knee
extensor moment. Altered movement patterns persist
following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
[12,13] despite surgical restoration of knee stability. This
suggests that instability is not the sole cause of the gait
adaptations.
While the literature provides some evidence that al-
tered joint angles and moments are compensations for
knee instability, it is conceivable that they are also the
result of quadriceps femoris strength deﬁcits. Quadri-
ceps strength deﬁcits are ubiquitous following both ACL
rupture [14–16], and ACL reconstruction [17–19], and
have been correlated with movement characteristics
during both walking [11,20] and jogging [11,21]. This
indicates that both instability and quadriceps strength
deﬁcits could be contributing to the gait deviations seen
in these patient populations.
ACL rupture has been associated with early degen-
erative changes to the articular cartilage of the knee
[1,22]. The instability that often accompanies an ACL
rupture may contribute to the development of articular
cartilage defects [23]. Degenerative changes also occur
after reconstructive surgery, despite the elimination of
the patient’s instability [1,22,23], which suggests that
instability is not the sole cause of the degenerative
changes. Quadriceps muscle weakness, which is preva-
lent in both ACL deﬁcient and reconstructed patients,
has recently been suggested to contribute to knee oste-
oarthritis [24]. If quadriceps femoris weakness contrib-
utes to altered movements and muscular adaptations,
then reduced quadriceps strength might also contribute
to the increased risk of arthritic changes in patient
populations following ACL rupture or reconstruction.
In addition, many of the gait deviations occur during
weight acceptance, when an eccentric quadriceps con-
traction is necessary to control knee ﬂexion and provide
shock absorption. So insuﬃcient quadriceps strength
could reduce the ability of the knee to attenuate shock,
which could lead to degenerative changes.
The purpose of this study was to investigate the eﬀect
of quadriceps femoris strength and instability on gait in
persons with anterior cruciate ligament rupture who
undergo operative stabilization. Those who have quad-
riceps weakness following surgery were expected to ex-
hibit diminished knee angles and reduced internal knee
extensor moments during weight acceptance, similar to
the adaptation that ACL deﬁcient subjects exhibit fol-
lowing injury [8]. Subjects with nearly normal quadri-
ceps strength following reconstruction were expected to
resume movement characteristics that are similar to
uninjured subjects.
2. Methods
2.1. Subjects
Twenty-eight individuals who had a complete isolated
tear of the anterior cruciate ligament and experienced
instability participated in this study. Instability was
objectively identiﬁed through a screening process de-
veloped by Fitzgerald et al. [4]. Ten of these 28 subjects
(six males, four females) were tested while still ACL
deﬁcient (ACL-D group) and were all less than 6 months
from the time of the injury. The other 18 individuals had
undergone a unilateral, endoscopic, arthroscopically
assisted ACL reconstruction by one of two surgeons
using a graft that did not violate the extensor mecha-
nism (i.e. allograft or double loop semitendinosis-grac-
ilis autograft). All subjects had knee instability prior to
reconstruction, but had clinically stable knees at the
time of testing (e.g. no buckling, shifting, or episodes of
giving way, normal Lachman and pivot shift tests).
These 18 subjects were divided into two groups based on
their quadriceps strength. Eight subjects (ﬁve males,
three females) comprised the strong-anterior cruciate
ligament reconstructed (ACLR) group, which was op-
erationally deﬁned as those with quadriceps strength of
90% or more in the involved limb compared to the un-
involved quadriceps. Ten subjects (four males, six fe-
males) comprised the weak-ACLR group which was
operationally deﬁned as those with 80% or less than that
of the uninvolved quadriceps (see Table 1). In a normal
population, less than a 10% side-to-side diﬀerence in
quadriceps strength can be expected, however, greater
than a 20% diﬀerence is considered abnormal [25]. All
subjects in the weak-ACLR group were tested at a
minimum of 12 weeks following surgery to allow for
ample time to recover quadriceps femoris strength. All
subjects in the ACL-D group and six individuals in each
of the ACL reconstructed groups were regular partici-
pants in activities involving jumping, pivoting, hard
cutting, or lateral movements prior to injury. The
remaining subjects were involved in either lower level
activities (jogging, running, or swimming) or were sed-
entary. Ten uninjured subjects (eight males, two
females), with no history of knee injury, were also tested
M. Lewek et al. / Clinical Biomechanics 17 (2002) 56–63 57

--- PAGE 3 ---
as a control group. All subjects were able to extend their
knees to at least zero degrees of extension, and had
sustained no damage to the contralateral knee. No
subject had knee pain or joint eﬀusion at the time of
testing. Patients with identiﬁed articular cartilage defects
or concomitant injury to other knee ligaments were ex-
cluded from the study. Subjects were included in the
study in order as they presented to our clinic, provided
they met all inclusion criteria. All subjects were in-
formed of the purpose of the study, and signed an in-
formed consent form, approved by the Human Subjects
Review Board of the University of Delaware, prior to
testing. All patients completed the Activities of Daily
Living Scale of the Knee Outcome Survey (KOS-
ADLS), a self-report of the function on the subject’s
knee to determine their level of knee instability [26].
2.2. Strength testing
Quadricepsstrengthwastestedasdescribedpreviously
[16,27]. Brieﬂy, each subject was seated on an isokinetic
dynamometer (KinCom, Chattanooga Group, Chatta-
nooga, TN, USA) and produced a four second maximum
voluntary isometric contraction with their knee ﬂexed to
90°. During this contraction, electrodes (ConMed, Utica,
NY, USA) placed over the quadriceps femoris muscle
produced a supramaximal burst of electrical current to
fully stimulate the quadriceps. If the subject failed to
generate volitional force within 95% of the electrically
elicited force, the test was repeated, up to four times with
5minrestbetweentests.Allsubjectswereabletoproduce
maximal force on both sides within one session and
therefore had no reﬂex inhibition. Both legs were tested
and the quadriceps index, a measure of relative strength,
was calculated (quadriceps index¼involved volitional
force/uninvolved volitional force  100).
2.3. Motion and electromyographic testing
Electromyographic (EMG) data were collected at 960
Hz using active surface electrodes with an eight-channel
hard-wired EMG system (Motion Lab Systems, Baton
Rouge, LA, USA) for the weak-ACLR and strong-
ACLR subjects, and an eight-channel telemetry EMG
system (B&L Engineering, Santa Fe Springs, CA, USA)
for the ACL-D and uninjured subjects. Elastic bands
(SuperWrape, Fabrifoam, Exton, PA, USA) were
wrapped over the electrodes to secure them bilaterally to
the muscle bellies of the medial head of the gastroc-
nemius, and mid-muscle belly of the lateral hamstrings
and vastus lateralis.
Motion testing was done with a six camera, passive,
three-dimensional motion analysis system (VICON,
Oxford Metrics, London, UK) recording at 120 Hz.
Calibration errors were kept below 3 mm. Force data
were recorded from a six-component force plate (Ber-
tec, Worthington, OH, USA) sampling at 960 Hz. The
cameras detected retro-reﬂective markers aﬃxed to the
subject’s shoes and placed in triads on rigid shells on
the posterior aspect of the pelvis, thigh, and shank.
Anatomical markers were placed over the head of the
ﬁfth metatarsal, lateral malleolus, lateral femoral con-
dyle, greater trochanters, and iliac crests. Motion,
force, and EMG data were collected concurrently as
subjects performed six trials of free-speed walking and
jogging along a 30-foot runway. Velocity data were
monitored with two photoelectric beams to ensure that
velocity varied not more than 5%. Trials were used if
the subject remained at a consistent velocity and landed
with their foot in the center of the force plate without
targeting.
2.4. Data management and analysis
Walking and jogging kinematic data were low-pass
ﬁltered at 6 and 10 Hz, respectively. Force plate data
were low-pass ﬁltered at 50 Hz. The marker clusters,
attached to the subject’s pelvis, thighs, shanks, and feet,
were used to track each segment’s three-dimensional
coordinate system. Move3D software (Move3D, NIH
Biomechanics Laboratory, Bethesda, MD, USA) was
used to calculate the knee’s sagittal plane motions.

--- PAGE 4 ---
Joint kinetics were calculated using inverse dynamics,
and are expressed as net internal moments. Knee angles
and moments were normalized to 100% of the stance
phase of gait. Joint moments were normalized to the
subject’s body mass multiplied by the leg length. The
subject’s six trials were averaged to obtain a mean for
each subject.
The strong-ACLR and weak-ACLR subjects’ raw
EMG data were band-pass ﬁltered between 20 and 350
Hz. Data from the ACL-D and uninjured group’s
muscles, collected with the telemetric system, were high-
pass ﬁltered with an eighth-order Butterworth ﬁlter at 90
Hz. For all groups, a linear envelope was created for
analysis using full-wave rectiﬁcation, followed by a
second-order, phase corrected low-pass Butterworth
ﬁlter with a cut-oﬀ frequency of 20 Hz. The linear en-
velope was normalized to the maximum muscle activity
recorded during either a dynamic or maximum volun-
tary isometric contraction trial. Custom-designed soft-
ware (Labview, National Instruments, Austin, TX,
USA) was used to calculate the integral of the muscle
activity from 100 ms prior to initial contact (to account
for electro-mechanical delay [28]) until peak knee ﬂex-
ion. All EMG data were compared to the subject’s un-
involved side. The diﬀerences in collection equipment
necessitated the need for diﬀerent ﬁltering parameters,
and therefore made it impossible to compare between
groups.
Group diﬀerences were determined using one-way
analyses of variance for the knee angle and moment at
both initial contact and peak knee ﬂexion. When dif-
ferences were detected, t-tests were used as post hoc tests
with a Bonferroni adjustment used to account for the
multiple comparisons performed; therefore, signiﬁcance
was set at p < 0:017. A MANOVA with two repeated
measures (muscle and side) was used to analyze the
EMG integral data within each group, however no
group comparisons were made because of the use of
diﬀerent EMG data collection systems. Regression an-
alyses were used to determine the relative eﬀect of
quadriceps strength and muscle activity on the knee
angles and moments at peak knee ﬂexion.
3. Results
There was no diﬀerence between the weak-ACLR and
strong-ACLR groups with respect to mean age
ðP ¼ 0:296Þ, mean time from surgery to testing
ðP ¼ 0:076Þ, or mean KOS-ADLS scores ðP ¼ 0:594Þ
(Table 1). The strong-ACLR group’s quadriceps index
of 95.3% was signiﬁcantly greater than the weak-ACLR
group’s quadriceps index of 67.6% ðP ¼ 0:000Þ, and the
ACL-D group’s 75.3% ðP ¼ 0:000Þ. There was no sig-
niﬁcant diﬀerence between the quadriceps indices of the
weak-ACLR and ACL-D groups ðP ¼ 0:140Þ.
4. Walking
There was no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the mean ve-
locity between groups ðP ¼ 0:089Þ. The weak-ACLR
and strong-ACLR subjects walked at 1.98 m/s/leg
length. The ACL-D group maintained 2.07 m/s/leg
length, while the uninjured subjects walked at 2.22 m/s/
leg length.
4.1. Kinematics and kinetics
The weak-ACLR, strong-ACLR, and ACL-D
groups’ knee angles at initial contact were not signiﬁ-
cantly diﬀerent from those of the uninjured group
ðP ¼ 0:729Þ (Table 2). At peak knee ﬂexion, the weak-
ACLR group showed a trend towards a diminished knee
angle ðP ¼ 0:043Þ (Fig. 1) and had a signiﬁcantly re-
duced knee moment ðP ¼ 0:001Þ (Fig. 2) compared to
the uninjured group. The ACL-D group had a trend
toward a decreased internal knee moment at peak knee
ﬂexion ðP ¼ 0:021Þ.
The ACL reconstructed subjects’ quadriceps index
accounted for a signiﬁcant portion of the variance in
knee angle ðP ¼ 0:036; R2
¼ 0:260Þ at peak knee ﬂex-
ion. Quadriceps index and the score on the KOS-ADLS
together accounted for a signiﬁcant portion of the
variance in the ACL reconstructed subjects’ knee mo-
ment at peak knee ﬂexion ðP ¼ 0:010; R2
¼ 0:604Þ.
4.2. Muscle activity
There were no signiﬁcant side-to-side diﬀerences in
EMG integrals for the medial gastrocnemius, vastus
lateralis, and lateral hamstrings for all patient groups.
5. Jogging
The weak-ACLR and strong-ACLR groups jogged at
3.36 and 3.48 m/s/leg length, respectively, during testing.
The ACL-D group jogged at 3.33 m/s/leg length, while
the uninjured group maintained 3.75 m/s/leg length.
There was no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the jogging speed
between groups ðP ¼ 0:485Þ.
5.1. Kinematics and kinetics
At initial contact, the patient groups’ knee angle was
not signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from that of the uninjured
group ðP ¼ 0:275Þ (Fig. 3). Both the weak-ACLR
ðP ¼ 0:056Þ and ACL-D ðP ¼ 0:063Þ groups showed a
trend towards a reduced knee ﬂexion angle at peak knee
ﬂexion. The internal knee extension moments of the
weak-ACLR ðP ¼ 0:003Þ, and ACL-D ðP ¼ 0:014Þ
groups were signiﬁcantly reduced compared to those of
the uninjured subjects at peak knee ﬂexion (Fig. 4). The
M. Lewek et al. / Clinical Biomechanics 17 (2002) 56–63 59

strong-ACLR group, however, was not diﬀerent from
that of the uninjured group in any kinematic or kinetic
variable we tested (Table 2).
There was a signiﬁcant relationship between the quad-
riceps index and the knee angle ðP ¼ 0:033; R2
¼ 0:254Þ
andmomentðP ¼ 0:006; R2

in the weak-ACLR and strong-ACLR subjects. The in-

Separation into the weak-ACLR and strong-ACLR

¼ 0:530Þ.
5.2. Muscle activity
The magnitudes of muscle activity in the vastus lat-
eralis and gastrocnemius muscles were not diﬀerent in
the involved and uninvolved sides of the weak-ACLR,
strong-ACLR, and ACL-D groups. The lateral ham-
strings, however, were signiﬁcantly more active in the
involved limb of the ACL-D group ðP ¼ 0:029Þ (Fig. 5).
6. Discussion
The hypothesis that quadriceps strength deﬁcits
contribute to the reduced knee angles and moments
during early stance in ACL deﬁcient and reconstructed
subjects was supported by the data, however, the muscle

--- PAGE 6 ---
activation patterns used to compensate for the altered
movements are diﬀerent. Only the strong group walked
and jogged similarly to the uninjured group. Those who
had quadriceps weakness following reconstructive sur-
gery had lower knee ﬂexion angles and internal knee
extensor moments during weight acceptance than unin-
jured subjects, similar to the adaptation that ACL de-
ﬁcient subjects exhibit following injury [7,8]. Subjects
with nearly normal quadriceps strength following re-
construction appeared to have suﬃcient eccentric
quadriceps control during weight acceptance to resume
normal knee movement patterns.
The weak-ACLR group’s walking and jogging
movement patterns strongly resembled those of the un-
stable ACL-D group, despite the surgical restoration of
knee stability. Both the weak and strong subjects had
undergone successful ACL reconstruction as manifested
by no symptoms of instability, full passive and active
knee range of motion, and no joint eﬀusion or pain. The
reduced knee angles and moments characteristic of the
gait of ACL deﬁcient individuals with instability, how-
ever, were present in the weak-ACLR group. These data
support the contention that quadriceps weakness con-
tributes to, but does not fully explain, the gait adapta-
tions in individuals with ACL injury.
The results of this study are consistent with the lit-
erature and help to complete the picture developed by
other investigators. DeVita et al. [13] reported that
despite 6 months of rehabilitation, subjects following
ACL reconstruction continued to have diminished knee
moments during early stance compared to controls.
Timoney and colleagues [29] also reported that fol-
lowing reconstruction, subjects exhibited diminished
knee moments during weight acceptance. Quadriceps
strength testing was not performed in these studies so
the relationship between quadriceps strength and de-
creased knee moment cannot be ascertained. Hurwitz
et al. [21] reported that the internal knee extension
moment during jogging was signiﬁcantly correlated
with isokinetic knee extension strength after ACL re-
construction. Snyder-Mackler et al. [20] reported that
isokinetic quadriceps indices were signiﬁcantly corre-
lated with ﬂexion excursion during the early stance
phase of walking in subjects following ACL recon-
struction. Our data conﬁrm the ﬁndings of all these
authors, and provide additional evidence that quadri-
ceps weakness contributes to the characteristic move-
ment patterns in these patients during both walking
and jogging.
The reduced knee extensor moments during weight
acceptance in the weak-ACLR group are not attribut-
able to reduced quadriceps activation, as vastus lateralis

--- PAGE 7 ---
muscle activities were not diﬀerent in the involved and
uninvolved sides. The full quadriceps activation found
in our weak-ACLR subjects is consistent with the ﬁnd-
ings of Bulgerhoni et al. [12], who reported greater
quadriceps activation during early stance in people fol-
lowing ACL reconstruction. During jogging, it appears
that the ACL-D subjects reduced the knee angles and
moments through an increase in hamstring activity. This
adaptation has been reported previously [30] as a com-
pensation for knee instability. The higher level of ham-
string muscle activation in the ACLD subjects suggests
that quadriceps femoris weakness exacerbates the
problem of knee instability and requires a diﬀerent
compensation strategy. It is important to note that none
of the groups demonstrated a signiﬁcant reduction in
quadriceps activity. The assertion that the reduced knee
extension moment that is seen in persons with ACL
injury represents an attempt to avoid episodes of insta-
bility by decreasing quadriceps activation is therefore
unsubstantiated using the current data.
The reduced knee ﬂexion in anterior cruciate ligament
deﬁcient and weak reconstructed subjects may have im-
portant consequences for long-term joint integrity. Re-
ducedkneeﬂexioninterfereswiththenormalabilityofthe
knee to absorb shock during weight acceptance [31], and
may be associated with early degenerative joint changes.
A stiﬀer knee, which does not ﬂex suﬃciently, is often
observed following ACL rupture or reconstruction
[8,12,13]. Our data provide evidence that quadriceps
strengthdeﬁcitsmaybeafactorinﬂuencingthisreduction
inkneeﬂexion,andthereforemightberesponsibleforthe
increased risk of early degenerative changes. Evidence
exists to suggest that the rate of loading, which was not
tested in this study, on articular cartilage may be more
detrimentaltothejointsurfacesthanthemagnitudeofthe
joint contact forces [32]. Quadriceps weakness has re-
cently been associated with an increased knee joint load-
ing rate in females [33], which bodes poorly for the
integrity of the joint’s contact surfaces.
Ifquadricepsfemorisstrengthdeﬁcitsareimplicatedin
thedevelopmentofearlydegenerativejointarthritis,then
return to high-level activity with weak quadriceps after
ACLreconstructionappearsilladvised.‘‘Returntoplay’’
guidelines are not clearly deﬁned following anterior cru-
ciate ligament reconstruction. While quadriceps femoris
strength is often used as a marker for rehabilitation pro-
gress, return to play criteria vary widely [34,35]. Shel-
bourne and Foulk [34] allow patients to return to sport
speciﬁc training with quadriceps index of 65%, but not to
return to full competition until the quadriceps index is
greaterthan80%.Othershaveusedacriterionmeasureof
a quadriceps index greater than 90% for return to sport
[35]. More recently, DeCarlo and colleagues [36] have
advocated a practice that allows patients to return to ac-
tivity when their knees have full range of motion, no ef-
fusion and the ‘‘knees can be rehabilitated to feeling
normal to them with everyday activities’’. All of the sub-
jects in our study met these criteria: they had self-ratings
of knee function that were high, no eﬀusion and normal
ROM.However,thegroupwithaquadricepsindexofless
than 80% had walking and jogging patterns that were
similar to patients with ACL deﬁciency, and these adap-
tations may be detrimental to joint integrity which sug-
gests that full ROM, no eﬀusion, and high self-rating
scoresoffunctionmaybeinsuﬃcientcriteriontoallowfor
‘‘return to play’’.
Clearly, knee instability aﬀects gait patterns [7,11].
Our data support the hypothesis that quadriceps femoris
strength deﬁcits also contribute signiﬁcantly to an al-
tered gait pattern after anterior cruciate ligament re-
construction. Strong quadriceps appear to be necessary
to allow for a return of normal joint kinematics, kinetics
and muscle activities following ACL reconstruction.
